newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions suspend walkouts over sick pay.
newsitem.headline: German unions suspend walkouts over sick pay.

text.p: A wave of industrial action in Germany against cuts in company sick-pay benefits was conditionally suspended on Monday after employers and unions agreed to meet again to discuss the controversial issue.

The metal and electronics industry employers' union Gesamtmetall said after an emergency meeting called to try to resolve the dispute that it was recommending its members to leave sick pay unchanged for the time being.
The metal and electronics trade union IG Metall urged its members not to stage protests at companies unless sick pay had actually been cut.
IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel said: "We are just as interested as Gesamtmetall in achieving as rapid a clarification of the situation as possible."
Zwickel said the aim of the talks, which will reconvene on October 10, was to ensure that "a very highly-explosive situation did not escalate."
The two sides met after attempts last week by major firms to implement a controversial law cutting benefits were met by mass protests.

Two of the companies worst-hit by wildcat strikes and protests, Daimler Benz and Ford said after the statement was issued that they would be suspending the imposition of sick-pay cuts during the talks.

"When you consider that 150,000 workers in the metal industry last week protested over this, it shows the level of indignation and rage that workers feel over this. In such a situation any solution will be complicated," Zwickel said.
Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe said after the reading of the joint statement the accord was "neutral for both sides."

Asked if this represented a less-aggressive stance on the issue, Stumpfe replied: "We have never taken an aggressive stance on this. It was IG Metall which acted aggressively with walkouts leading to millions of marks of losses."
Dieter Hundt, vice-president of Gesamtmetall, said employers had for weeks been inviting IG Metall to discuss a new law seeking to trim sick pay costs by 20 percent.

"The metal and electronics industry does not need a hot autumn but cool heads," Hundt told German radio, referring to the hot autumn of industrial unrest that many union leaders have been threatening.
IG Metall vice chairman Walter Riester said at the weekend that Germany would see "tougher strikes than the country has ever experienced" if no agreement was reached on the matter.
The talks took place at a hotel just outside Frankfurt.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday repeated calls for the two sides to debate the issue sensibly and criticised them for not having attempted to reach a consensus earlier.

Employers and unions were seen as initially seeking to defuse tension on the issue, particularly with IG Metall due to announce its overall 1997 wage demands for the 3.5 million workers it represents on Tuesday.
One possible compromise between employers and workers is seen as replacing the envisaged 20 percent cut in sick pay benefits with a corresponding reduction in holiday.
An employee would thus continue to get 100 percent of salary while ill but would lose one day of holiday for each five days sick.
A similar system has already been put into practice at carmaker Audi AG, a unit of Volkswagen AG, where workers will accrue "time debts" either to be worked off or paid back.
